summary: This document sets out requirements for Content Distribution Network Interconnection. As more providers build their own CDNs, they need ways to deliver content across each other's networks, for example when a user is outside the footprint of the CDN contracted by the content provider.

plainLanguage.summary: Content may need to cross several separately operated content delivery networks before it reaches a user. This RFC lists requirements for those networks to coordinate routing, delivery rules, and records.

questions: what is an upstream cdn and downstream cdn
subtitle: Requirements for separate content delivery networks to serve users as one delivery platform.

tldr.problem: A content request may need to pass through more than one independently operated content delivery network, so those networks need to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists prioritized requirements for control, request routing, footprint and capability exchange, metadata, logging, and security.
tldr.outcome: This Informational document states requirements for a CDNI solution and interfaces; it does not define their protocols.

today: RFC 7337 is an Informational requirements document published in August 2014. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it; the RFC states requirements rather than defining the CDNI protocols.

sections.title: Why Content Delivery Networks Interconnect
sections.content:
Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) serve content from distributed infrastructure. As multiple service providers build CDNs, a content item may need to cross between them to reach a user, subject to the content provider's policy. The CDNI working group was chartered to develop an interoperable and scalable solution.

RFC 7337 collects requirements for that solution. It labels requirements HIGH, MED, or LOW: HIGH is essential even if it delays a deployable solution; MED should be met unless it causes delay; LOW is pursued when it does not block higher priorities.
sections.plainLanguage: Separate CDNs need a way to cooperate when one network cannot serve a user's request alone. This RFC ranks the capabilities that an interconnection solution should provide.

sections.title: The CDNI Interfaces
sections.content:
The model has an Upstream CDN that passes work to a Downstream CDN. The Control interface bootstraps other interfaces and can trigger actions such as pre-positioning or purging content. Request routing determines which CDN or Surrogate serves a request, using footprint and capability information and a redirection exchange.

The Metadata interface carries rules that govern delivery, such as geographic restrictions or availability windows. The Logging interface exchanges records of activity, for monitoring, analysis, or billing. The RFC refers to RFC 7336 for the definitive model.
sections.plainLanguage: The CDNs need separate ways to coordinate setup, routing, delivery rules, and activity records. The RFC calls these the Control, Request Routing, Metadata, and Logging interfaces.

sections.title: Generic and Control Requirements
sections.content:
The generic requirements say the solution should reuse existing IETF protocols where possible. It must not require changes to a user's software or to a content provider that uses one CDN, and it must not require a CDN to reveal internal details such as its Surrogate topology or cached content. The solution must support HTTP delivery and acquisition and prevent loops in information exchange.

The Control interface must let an Upstream CDN request that the Downstream CDN delete its objects or metadata, including across cascaded CDNs. The Downstream CDN must report whether the action succeeded. Other control functions, including pre-positioning, are assigned lower priority in the requirement list.
sections.plainLanguage: Interconnection should work without forcing content providers or users to change how they operate. It must also let a CDN request deletion of its own content and learn whether the request succeeded.

sections.title: Routing and Capabilities
sections.content:
Request Routing requirements cover efficient choices for small and large objects. A lighter DNS-style decision may trade some freshness or accuracy for lower load; a per-request HTTP-style decision may be appropriate when a fresh choice matters. The interface must support recursive and iterative routing and must support routing each chunk of HTTP Adaptive Streaming content.

The Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement interface lets a Downstream CDN report whether it can accept work and describe information such as its network footprint, supported content types, protocols, resources, and preferences. The advertised fields must be extensible so the information can grow.
sections.plainLanguage: CDNs need to decide where each request should go and whether the chosen network can serve it. The RFC allows different routing styles and requires the capability information to support extensions.

sections.title: Metadata and Logs
sections.content:
The Metadata interface must support both dynamic and pre-positioned metadata. Metadata may apply to one object or a group, and more specific rules take precedence over broader ones. It can describe acquisition sources, authorization checks, geographic restrictions, availability windows, and delegation rules. Conflicting rules with overlapping scope must be prevented or resolved deterministically.

The Logging interface must reliably transfer records about completed and incomplete deliveries, support batch or offline exchange, and define a format and transport. Near-real-time exchange is a medium-priority requirement. Privacy protection, such as anonymizing an IP address in a record, is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: Delivery rules can apply to one item or a group, with precise rules taking priority over general ones. Logs tell the partner what happened, and the requirements allow optional privacy protection.

sections.title: Security Requirements
sections.content:
All CDNI interfaces must support secure operation over an unsecured IP network. The requirements include authentication, confidentiality, integrity protection, and protection against spoofing and replay. The solution must also protect against denial-of-service attacks, including requests that falsely claim to have been redirected by an Upstream CDN.

Other requirements aim to let a Downstream CDN identify the CDN that redirected a request and let an Upstream CDN check that a received log record corresponds to one of its redirections. The Security Considerations section points readers to these requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Each CDN must be able to verify its partner and protect information sent between them. The requirements also address fake redirections and false delivery records.
